title: Duty and the coward (2.26–2.38)
hook: Krishna comes down from eternity to earth: death is certain, this is your work, and people will talk
tomorrow: "You have the right to act, never to the fruit" (2.39–2.53)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the self that is not slain: never born, never dies, and bodies like worn-out clothes. Your line was never born, never dies. What carried over, in the old photo? Today, Krishna comes down to earth. Day one hundred sixty-three.

Good teachers do something you'll recognize. They give you the big, beautiful idea. Then they look at your face, see it hasn't quite landed, and try again from a completely different angle, something plainer, closer to the ground. Krishna has just told Arjuna about the eternal self, weapons that can't cut it, fire that can't burn it. Arjuna is still sitting there. So Krishna changes gear. Fine, he says, in effect. Suppose you don't believe any of that. Here's why you still shouldn't grieve, and why you still have to stand up.
screen: `THE BIG IDEA DIDN'T LAND.` → `KRISHNA CHANGES GEAR.` → `SUPPOSE YOU DON'T BELIEVE IT.`

segments.voice: Argument one: even if you think the self is born and dies all the time, still don't grieve. In Sanskrit: jatasya hi dhruvo mrityur, dhruvam janma mritasya cha. For the one who is born, death is certain; for the one who dies, birth is certain. You can't change what's inevitable. Beings are unseen before they're born, seen in the middle, and unseen again at the end. What is there to lament? Argument two: dharma. Look at your own dharma, Krishna says, your svadharma, the duty that's yours. Arjuna is a kshatriya, a warrior whose role is to protect, and this, Krishna says, is a righteous fight. Refuse it, and you abandon what's yours. Argument three, and this one stings: people will talk. The great warriors will think you ran from fear. Your enemies will say things that shouldn't be said. For someone honored, dishonor is worse than death. You may notice these three get more and more down to earth. Commentators notice it too; some say Krishna is meeting Arjuna where he is, before the deeper teaching. Then comes the verse that turns toward that teaching. Sukha dukhe same kritva, labhalabhau jayajayau. Treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as the same, and then act. Readers take this battlefield in different ways. Some read it as a real war and a real duty. Gandhi read the whole Gita as a teaching about an inner fight, and drew nonviolence from it. Either way, the core holds: there's work that's yours, and running from it doesn't make you free.
screen: `DEATH IS CERTAIN FOR THE BORN.` · `SVADHARMA: THE DUTY THAT'S YOURS.` · `PEOPLE WILL TALK.` · `WIN OR LOSE, THE SAME. THEN ACT.` · then, large: `THERE'S WORK THAT'S YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find what's yours. Settle, and breathe. Think of the roles you actually hold right now. Parent. Friend. Nurse. Student. The one who keeps the family talking. Pick one. Now ask: what's the piece of work in that role that only I can do, and that I've been avoiding? Don't judge it. Just see it clearly. Then try on Krishna's line: win or lose, the same. Picture doing that work without needing it to go well. Just because it's yours. Breathe there. The bell holds the time.
Duty and the coward. Death is certain for the born, there's work that's yours, and win or lose, you do it anyway.
Your line: do what's yours. Today, do the one piece of work that belongs to you and no one else, and let the result be what it is. Day one hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 163 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE RIGHT TO ACT, NOT THE FRUIT.`

howItsDone: Hindus often draw on Gita 2.31–2.38 when speaking of svadharma, the duty that belongs to one's own role and stage of life, and 2.38's call to treat gain and loss, victory and defeat alike is widely quoted.

match.prompt: Krishna's three arguments, and one turn — tap the pairs.
pairs: death is certain for the born

myth: Krishna only argues from the eternal self
he also argues from plain facts: death is certain, this is your duty, people will talk.
Gandhi read the Gita's battle as an inner fight
and he drew nonviolence from it. others read it as a real war and a real duty.
2.38 says to act only when you're sure to win
it says to treat gain and loss, victory and defeat as the same, and then act.

fork.setup: you're Krishna. you've taught Arjuna the eternal self, and he's still sitting down. what do you try next?
options: come down to earth: death is certain, this is your work.
give up and fight in his place.
fork.reveal: he changes gear: even if you don't believe it, death is certain for the born, this duty is yours, and people will talk. then: win or lose, the same.

original.note: Sanskrit: sva, one's own, and dharma. the duty that belongs to you.

trapdoor: what you thought: Krishna shames Arjuna into fighting.
what it means: Krishna meets Arjuna where he is, with plainer and plainer reasons, then turns: win or lose, the same, and act.
what a scholar hears: commentators often read 2.31–2.37 as a lower, worldly argument that sets up the higher teaching beginning at 2.39.

notes: Kshatriya duty and 'a righteous fight' (dharmya yuddha, 2.31); the script names Arjuna's varna without discussing the varna system. Confirm framing.
2.32 (a door to heaven) and 2.37 (slain, heaven; victorious, the earth) are not mentioned. Confirm omission is acceptable.
'Commentators notice... Krishna is meeting Arjuna where he is': a general characterization (e.g. many modern commentators). Confirm.
The title's word 'coward' is the outline's; the script avoids calling Arjuna a coward. Confirm.
Editor review 2026-10-01: 'many [commentators] say' softened to 'some say'.
